name: Shoulder Press
family: Overhead press, machine (difference card of machine_chest_press, mode D per LIB-HT 6.2)

inherit.why: true for this child because ACE gives the same full grip with the thumbs clasped around the handles for the machine shoulder press (c2) as for the machine chest press, and the thumb does the same job of keeping the handle out of the fingers.
true for this child because the press still runs along the forearm into the heel of the palm (push archetype, loadAxis along-forearm); only the direction changes from forward to up.
true for this child because ACE asks for the same neutral wrist, in line with the forearm, at the start and all the way up (c2, c5).

inherit.field: setup['Pick the weight. Start lighter than you think; if you have to bend your wrist back to hold it, it is too heavy.']
inherit.why: true for this child because the wrist-fold fault it guards against comes from the same handle, grip and push line.
true for this child because the hand on the handle and the bent-back-wrist fault look the same; the forearm is simply vertical instead of horizontal.

claims.text: Sit with the back firmly against the backrest and set the seat so the handles are level with, or just higher than, the shoulders.

quotes.text: Sit with your back firmly supported against the backrest. Adjust the seat height so that the handles are level with your shoulders or just higher than your shoulders.

claims.text: Hold the handles firmly with a full grip, thumbs wrapped, wrists in line with the forearms.

quotes.text: Grasp the handles firmly with a full grip (thumbs clasped around the handles) and maintain a neutral wrist position (i.e., wrists in line with your forearms).

claims.text: The elbows sit slightly in front of the body (the 4 and 8 o'clock position), not straight out to the sides.

quotes.text: Position your elbows in the 4 and 8 o'clock position (i.e., slightly forward than the 3 and 9 o'clock positions where the elbows are aligned with the midline of your trunk).

claims.text: Feet planted; brace the stomach and keep the natural low-back curve without pressing the low back into the pad and without arching; shoulders held back and down.

quotes.text: Position your feet firmly on the floor or on the foot rests to stabilize your body.

Stiffen (“brace”) your abdominal muscles to stabilize your spine, but do not press your low back into the backrest. Maintain the natural arch in your low back and avoid arching your back throughout the exercise.
Depress and retract your scapulae (pull shoulders back and down) and attempt to hold this position throughout the exercise.

claims.text: Breathe out and press slowly up, head in line with the spine and without arching the low back.

quotes.text: Gently exhale and slowly perform an upward pressing movement, extending your elbows overhead while maintaining a neutral wrist position, head aligned with your spine and avoidng arching your low back.

claims.text: Press until the elbows are straight but not locked, pause briefly, then lower slowly, using the back muscles (lats) to draw the handles down rather than letting them drop, because the shoulder is relatively unstable overhead.

quotes.text: Continue pressing until your elbows are fully extended, but not locked.
Pause momentarily then gently contract your lats (back muscles) to pull the handles back down towards your starting position, allowing your elbows to flex (bend) in a slow, controlled manner

In the overhead position, the shoulder is relatively unstable. To protect your shoulder it is important to engage your lats (back muscles) to initiate the downward movement as oppsed to simply yielding to gravity.

claims.text: Pointing the elbows forward on the close handles shifts load from the shoulders to the triceps; ACE calls it more comfortable for people who feel discomfort in the standard press.

quotes.text: This position shifts more of the load into the triceps and away from the shoulders.

This position is more comfortable and less stressful on the shoulders and more appropriate for individuals who experience some discomfort when performing traditional shoulder presses as it shifts more load into the triceps.

claims.text: In the sitting military press (equipment not stated in the abstract), the widest range (elbows fully straight at the top) raised activity in all the muscles recorded, including the shoulder muscles, triceps, trapezius and clavicular chest, compared with stopping at 90 degrees.

quotes.text: The results showed that the use of the widest ROM increased the EMG activity of all the muscles selected with respect to the closest one

Electromyographic surface electrodes were placed on the clavicular head of pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, medial deltoid (MD), posterior deltoid (PD), upper trapezius, middle trapezius (MT), long head of triceps, and teres minor (TM).

claims.text: In 31 healthy young adults with no resistance-training experience, on a machine shoulder press, focusing on the deltoids raised deltoid activity and focusing on the triceps raised triceps activity, while upper trapezius activity did not change.

quotes.text: Thirty-one healthy young adults with no athletic or resistance training experience participated in this single-session study.

Post hoc analysis showed that DT activity was higher in the DT-focused condition, whereas TB activity was higher in the TB-focused condition (p < 0.001). UT activity did not differ across conditions (p > 0.05).
Participants performed machine-based shoulder presses at 40% of one-repetition maximum intensity under three MMC conditions.

claims.text: In military presses with an open grip (equipment not stated in the abstract), the front delt was very active, while the upper (clavicular) chest was mostly inactive in almost all versions. Applied to the machine by similarity; it conflicts with c8, which recorded the upper chest working.

quotes.text: The results showed high inactivity for PMC in almost all the modalities while DA developed very high levels of action potentials in all the modalities assessed.

claims.text: In five experienced bodybuilders lifting to failure at 80-100% of their maximum (single-arm curls, overhead presses, single- and double-leg presses), blood pressure rose to extremely high values during each lift, highest in the double-leg press; part of the rise was caused by breath holding (a Valsalva manoeuvre). That breathing out through the effort keeps pressure lower is reasoning; the study did not test it.

quotes.text: The purpose of this study was to record the blood pressure response to heavy weight-lifting exercise in five experienced body builders.
Exercises included single-arm curls, overhead presses, and both double- and single-leg presses performed to failure at 80, 90, 95, and 100% of maximum.
Systolic and diastolic blood pressures rose rapidly to extremely high values during the concentric contraction phase for each lift
The greatest peak pressures occurred during the double-leg press where the mean value for the group was 320/250 mmHg, with pressures in one subject exceeding 480/350 mmHg.
indicate that a portion of the observed increase in blood pressure was caused by a Valsalva maneuver.

claims.text: For intermediate to advanced lifters with an eventual emphasis on heavy loads (1-6 RM), ACSM advises a moderate speed of 1-2 seconds up and 1-2 seconds down; the plate uses it only as a drawing convention for tempo. Load goes up by 2-10% once the target reps are beaten by one or two.

quotes.text: with eventual emphasis on heavy loading (1-6 RM) using 3- to 5-min rest periods between sets performed at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)
When training at a specific RM load, it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.

plate.viewWhy: The press is vertical in the sagittal plane and the plate fault, the low back arching off the pad (c4, c5), reads only from the side. The 4-and-8 o'clock elbow position (c3) is a top-view detail and goes to text.
plate.equipment: Seated shoulder press machine: upright back pad, seat, pivot-arm handles that start at or just above shoulder height (c1) and travel up (census: same lever primitive, overhead arm path).
plate.start: Seated upright, back on the pad with the natural low-back curve (c1, c4); feet planted (c4); handles level with or just above the shoulders (c1); elbows bent under the hands and slightly in front of the trunk (c3); wrists straight (c2).
plate.end: Arms overhead, elbows straight but not locked (c6); head in line with the spine (c5); low-back curve unchanged, no arch (c4, c5); shoulders still down (c4).

checkpoints.label: Handles at shoulders
checkpoints.what: The seat puts the handles level with or just above the shoulders at the start.

checkpoints.label: No back arch
checkpoints.what: The low back keeps its natural curve against the pad and does not arch as you press.

checkpoints.label: Soft elbows overhead
checkpoints.what: The press ends with the elbows straight but not locked.

mistake.what: Arching the low back off the pad to push the handles up.
mistake.why: ACE warns against it in the setup and again during the press.

tells.text: Low-back curve unchanged at the top

plate.variantLine: The plate draws the standard handles with the elbows slightly in front of the trunk (c3). The sources do not say which way the palms face on either handle pair; the engine's pivot-arm primitive draws a neutral grip, so a wide-handle option is an equipment gap for the supervisor. The close-handle option (c7) keeps every other rule: same seat, grip, brace, press, lockout and lowering (c1, c2, c4, c5, c6).

grip.type: Full grip on the machine's handles (c2). The standard handles with the elbows at 4 and 8 o'clock are drawn (c3); the close handles with the elbows pointing forward are the shoulder-friendlier option (c7). Palm direction is not given by the sources.
grip.width: Set by the machine's handle pair; elbows slightly in front of the trunk (c3).

setup.step: Set the seat so the handles are level with or just above your shoulders.
Sit back against the pad, feet planted; brace, keep the natural low-back curve, shoulders back and down.
Take the handles with a full grip, thumbs round, wrists straight.
If the standard press bothers your shoulders, use the close handles with the elbows pointing forward.
Add 2-10% load only when you can do one or two reps more than your target.

posture.point: Elbows slightly in front of the body, not straight out to the sides.
Breathe out as you press; don't hold your breath through the set.
Head in line with the spine.
No arching of the low back.
Elbows straight but not locked at the top.
Draw the handles down slowly with the back muscles.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Arching the low back off the pad to finish the press.
handlingMistakes.fix: Brace and keep the natural curve. If you can't press without arching, lower the weight.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Letting the handles drop on the way down.
handlingMistakes.fix: Draw them down slowly with your back muscles.
Stop just before the elbows lock, pause, then lower.

rows.where: Front or top of the shoulder, sharp or pinching
rows.means: The shoulder is relatively unstable in the overhead position.
rows.fix: Stop the set. Next session, you can try the close handles with the elbows pointing forward.

rows.means: The lower-back fault to watch here is arching off the pad.
rows.fix: Brace, keep the natural curve, lower the weight.

rows.means: The elbow rule here is to stop short of locking.

risks.risk: The shoulder is relatively unstable overhead; lower under control, never let the handles drop.
Arching the low back off the pad to finish reps.
Very heavy lifts to failure, overhead presses included, sent blood pressure extremely high in a small group of lifters, partly from breath holding.

zooms.right: Natural low-back curve against the pad, arms overhead, elbows soft.
zooms.wrong: Low back arched away from the pad.

zooms.right: Handles level with or just above the shoulders at the start.

libraryDiff.why: exercises.json lists front_delts and side_delts primary, triceps and upper_chest secondary. c8, c9 and c10 support the delts and triceps. For upper_chest the evidence conflicts: c8 recorded more clavicular-chest activity with the full range, while c10 found it mostly inactive in almost all versions (both seated or military presses, equipment not stated in the abstracts). The card's feel spec therefore leaves upper_chest out, and the library entry is left as is, with the conflict flagged.

tierA.thumb: Wrapped, full grip (c2); no thumbless option offered.
tierA.loadWording: Where the load causes the fault, the fix says to lower the weight (content.md 5.2 load wording); the sharp or pinching shoulder row says to stop the set (c6), with the close handles only as a next-session option (c7). No fix says to push through pain.
tierA.warningLink: Shoulder row links the shoulder box (c6).
tierA.risks: Three risk lines, including the shared breath line (c11).
tierA.loadProgression: Setup step: add 2-10% only when you beat your target reps by one or two (c12).

notes: Mode D per the plan: derived from the machine chest press plate. content.md appendix A lists shoulder_press as a parent on its own; the supervisor's brief makes it a difference card of machine_chest_press, and the shared parts (same push hand and lever primitive) justify the inherit lines above. ACE's text has typos ('avoidng', 'oppsed'), kept verbatim in quotes. The EMG claims come from military presses whose equipment the abstracts do not state (Paoli 2010, Bull 2010), tagged MECH or WEAK, and one machine study (Kim 2026). No source was found for a safe way to fail a rep (tier-A way out); see gaps.
gaps: Tier A way out: no source read says how to fail a rep safely on a shoulder press machine; left out of the sheet, not invented.
Tier A: safeties or J-hooks and a bar path clear of the neck do not apply as written to a pivot-arm machine; no source read describes the handle arc's clearance from the head or face.
Palm direction on the handles is not given by any source read (see plate.variantLine).

No source on this card says what to do if a sharp shoulder pinch keeps coming back; the row fix does not add one. The shared shoulder red-flag box and the owner disclaimer carry the stop-and-check line.
